title: Factual recall in linear associative memories: sharp asymptotics and mechanistic insights
claim: A simplified problem variant with independent competing outputs is equally hard as the original, sharing the same capacity threshold.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: two key-value diagrams, then accuracy plot with threshold line
description: The left two panels are labelled boxes, 'Original Problem' and 'Decoupled Problem'. Each shows a column of colored 'Keys' cells (Tokyo, Cairo, Rome, Paris) with dotted arrows to 'Values' cells (Italy, Egypt, France, Japan). In the original panel, all keys map into one shared Values column. In the decoupled panel, the Values column becomes a fanned stack of offset cards, one per key. Each card holds its own distractor outputs in grey (Korea, Turkey, Brazil) plus the correct one. The right panel is a line plot of Accuracy (y) against load alpha (x, 0.4 to 1.0). Accuracy stays at 1.0 until about 0.75, then falls. Solid (original) and dashed (decoupled) curves for d=50 to 500 use a purple-to-green gradient and nearly overlap. A red dashed vertical line marks alpha_c=1/2. The legend sits above the plot.
caption: Left: The task is to memorise associations between inputs (keys) and outputs (values), illustrated here as cities and their countries. In the original problem, all inputs share a common set of outputs. In the decoupled problem, each input has its own independent set of competing outputs. Right: Empirical accuracy as a function of the load parameter $\alpha = p \log p / d^2$, shown for the original problem [ref] (solid), the decoupled problem [ref] (dashed), across several embedding dimensions $d$. The original and decoupled problems appear consistently equally hard, suggesting a common capacity threshold. Models are trained with Adam on the cross-entropy loss (see [ref]). The red dashed line marks the asymptotic threshold $\alpha_c = 1/2$ of both problems ([ref]), which the transitions approach slowly due to finite-size effects of order $O((\log p)^{-1})$, see [ref].
abstract: Large language models excel at factual recall, yet the fundamental limits of storing input--output associations with neural networks remain unclear. We study these limits in a minimal setting: a linear associative memory that maps $p$ input embeddings in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to their $d$-dimensional targets via a linear layer, requiring each mapped input to score its own target above all other outputs. Since all inputs compete for the same outputs, these constraints are strongly correlated, which makes the storage capacity $p_c$ --- the largest number of associations that can be stored --- hard to characterise. We address this in three steps. First, we introduce a decoupled model, in which each input competes with its own independent set of outputs, and provide numerical and analytical evidence that it is equivalent to the original model, both in capacity and in the structure of the learnt solution. Second, using tools from statistical physics, we show that the decoupled model has capacity $p_c \log p_c / d^2 = 1/2$, extend this computation to linear two-layer networks, and go beyond the capacity by predicting the spectrum of the learnt weights and the storage mechanism. The latter explains how the optimal solution outperforms a naÃ¯ve Hebbian rule: rather than boosting input--output alignments with broad fluctuations, it raises the correct scores just above the extreme-value threshold set by the competing outputs. Third, we prove the decoupled model's capacity thresholds rigorously, including in the non-convex two-layer case; combined with a recent proof for the original model, this shows that both models have the same capacity for full-rank weights. These findings give a sharp characterisation of factual storage in linear networks, and suggest decoupling as a general tool for memorisation and learning problems in which each input must be matched to one of an extensive number of outputs.
